title: Supernewsjunkies?
hook: Updating is not a virtue by itself. Any change in an estimate can be called an update. The question is whether the move was the right size for the signal that triggered it. Move too little and the old evidence holds more weight than it deserves. Move too much and you hand the new signal more power than it has earned.
counterintuition: What distinguishes careful forecasters from those consuming the same headlines and reaching less accurate estimates? The gap is not volume of consumption. It is the ratio of diagnostic content extracted to narrative noise discarded, and that ratio improves with practice, not with more subscriptions. A vivid, detail-rich report can produce worse estimates than a single sentence of clean diagnostic data, because the detail activates the illusion of evidence without adding predictive weight.
tryThisNow: The next time you read a report or article, count how many sentences contain new diagnostic information versus contextual detail and repetition. Identify the one or two diagnostic sentences. Ask how much your estimate would move if those sentences were verified. Write the number. That is your proportionate update, not the emotional salience of the whole document.
keyTakeaway: Update quality matters more than frequency. Strip the narrative from the signal and move the estimate by exactly what the diagnostic content has earned, no more and no less.

breakdown.fastRead:
Ryan had been at 45% acquittal before the statement arrived. Six pages, typed, confident, first paragraph reading like the defense opening she had been hoping someone had seen.

She did not move to 70%.

The witness had testified in another case two years earlier and been cleanly impeached on a detail that mattered. The statement was real. The supporting force was real. The impeachment risk was also real. She worked through it: the statement added direct weight but the impeachment risk discounted that weight. She moved to 51%.

The new evidence did not change the story. It added one small piece to it. The estimate moved by exactly as much as that piece earned.
breakdown.deepRead:
Bill Flack's 5-percentage-point revision was not timid. It was accurate. The polonium story was suggestive, not conclusive, and a 5-point move was what the evidence had earned.

The signal was meaningful. The story emerged from a medical investigation, not rumor, and the testing methodology had genuine credibility. But meaningful and conclusive are not the same thing. The polonium could have been incidental exposure rather than administered. The investigation had not reported a final finding. The probability that Arafat died of state-sponsored poisoning should move upward. By how much? Enough to reflect that a real investigation had found a real result with some but not complete diagnostic weight. Five points.

Most analysts facing the same news would have either discounted it entirely or moved dramatically. Discounting entirely would have been anchoring to the prior story. Moving dramatically would have been granting the story more evidentiary force than it had. Both are forms of error. Flack's move was the narrow path between them.

Update sizing is not a skill that feels good to execute. Moving 5 points on news that feels like it should produce certainty is uncomfortable. That discomfort is information: it is the gap between the emotional salience of the news and its actual diagnostic value. The discomfort does not mean the move was too small. It means the move was honest.
breakdown.fullRead:
Tim Minto's forecasting log looked like a gentle staircase: many small steps rather than the cliffs and plateaus that mark a forecaster who holds and then panics.

The staircase pattern was not caution. It was calibration. Each small step reflected what each piece of evidence had actually earned. When a signal was small, the move was small. When a signal was larger, the move was larger. The staircase was steep or shallow in proportion to the evidence rather than in proportion to how dramatically the news had been reported.

The dilution effect runs in the opposite direction. A detail-rich report with vivid imagery and named sources creates a sense of comprehensive intelligence. That feeling of richness is real. The diagnostic content is not proportionate to the feeling.

Here is the mechanism: a detailed, narrative-rich information package activates the same cognitive responses as a detailed, diagnostic information package. The mind cannot easily distinguish between 'this contains a lot of information' and 'this contains a lot of information that actually changes the estimate.' The detail makes the case feel stronger. The emotional weight of a confident, textured account is higher than the emotional weight of a single clear sentence. But the single clear sentence is often what actually moves the needle, while the many paragraphs of context merely carry it.

Catarina's 47-page transcript yielded one sentence of genuinely revised forward guidance. One sentence in 47 pages. But the experience of reading 47 pages made it hard to hold onto the fact that most of the update work was done by that one sentence. The full package felt like an avalanche of information. The diagnostic content was a small movement in one direction. The update was 4 percentage points, not 24.

Overreaction and underreaction are mirror failures. Overreaction grants too much power to a new signal: the vivid story arrives and the estimate swings in its direction beyond what the evidence warrants. Underreaction refuses to grant the signal the weight it has actually earned: the estimate sits still while evidence accumulates unacknowledged. Both errors show up in track records. Overreaction produces estimates that move in the right direction but overshoot. Underreaction produces estimates that move too late, after the period where early calibration would have mattered.

The discipline is to strip the narrative before sizing the update. Not after reading. If you read the whole document and then ask how much should this move my estimate, the vividness of the narrative has already contaminated the answer. The question to ask before reading any detailed report is: what would I need to see to change my estimate, and by how much? Then read to find whether that appears. What appears determines the move. Everything else is context.

examples.title: Ryan moves from 45% to 51% acquittal probability after a strong but impeachable witness statement

planSpec.domain: criminal defense attorney receiving a new witness statement two weeks before trial
planSpec.audience: a defense lawyer whose acquittal probability assessment is 45% before the statement arrives
planSpec.stakes: whether to pursue a plea deal or continue to trial based on the new evidence
planSpec.requiredBeat: lawyer reasons through the impeachment risk and moves 45% to 51% rather than 70%

examples.scenario:
The manila folder is on the table, six pages inside it, the first paragraph already making the case sound stronger. Ryan reads it twice. A witness who places the defendant at a different location at the time the prosecution says the incident occurred. The testimony is clear, confident, and detailed.

She sets the folder down and asks the question she has learned to ask first: how much should this actually move the estimate?

The witness had testified in a civil proceeding two years earlier. Opposing counsel had impeached a specific timeline claim, and the witness had recanted that portion under cross-examination. The impeachment was on record, discoverable, and the prosecution would find it.

The statement adds corroborating force. That is real. But a statement from a witness who can be impeached on a prior inconsistency has reduced credibility weight. She works through the adjustment: the statement alone, from a clean witness, might move the acquittal estimate from 45% to somewhere around 60% to 65%. The impeachment risk discounts that by roughly half. The net move is to 51%.

The plea deadline is 36 hours away. Ryan must decide: treat the statement as strong enough to walk away from the current plea terms, or keep both options open while the impeachment risk is weighed. She continues to negotiate in parallel, keeping the plea option open at current terms while trial preparation advances.
examples.whatToDo: When a new piece of evidence arrives, ask how much it would move the estimate from a credible, unimpeachable source before applying any discounts for reliability concerns. Then apply those discounts explicitly. The move is from the adjusted credibility-weighted value, not from the face value of the testimony.
examples.whyItMatters: An unexamined reaction to a vivid witness statement produces a much larger move than the evidence warrants. A statement that feels like a breakthrough but comes from a witness who can be impeached on prior inconsistency is worth considerably less than the emotional salience of the new information suggests. Working through the discount before updating prevents the estimate from moving too far on evidence that has real limitations.

examples.title: Nina holds the broader contamination estimate at 42% after a single new cluster and recommends one more day of sampling

planSpec.domain: epidemiologist updating an active outbreak model after a single new geographically clustered case cluster
planSpec.audience: a field epidemiologist tracking a foodborne illness cluster across two counties
planSpec.stakes: whether to issue a broader public warning affecting twelve businesses in a third county
planSpec.requiredBeat: supervisor wants to issue warning immediately; epidemiologist moves from 35% to 42% probability of broader contamination and recommends one more day of sampling

examples.scenario:
'I've already drafted the warning,' the supervisor says over the phone. 'The third-county cluster confirms it. I need you to sign off.'

Nina is looking at the cluster data on her screen. Four cases in the third county, confirmed in the past 48 hours, geographically distinct from the two-county cluster she has been tracking.

'Give me a number first,' she says.

She has been at 35% probability of broader regional contamination. The new cluster is real. But single geographic extensions in foodborne outbreaks are not always connected to the index cluster. The base rate of false geographic extensions, where a concurrent but independent cluster appears near an active one, runs at roughly 25% to 30% in the literature for this pathogen type. The new cluster should move the estimate. By how much?

The cluster is four cases, not twenty. It is one cluster, not three independent reports from across the region. She calculates: the single cluster raises the probability to approximately 42%, not to 80%.

'I'm at 42% broader contamination,' she tells the supervisor. 'That's up from 35%. It is not at the threshold for a regional warning. If we get a second independent cluster tomorrow from a different town, that moves it. One more day of sampling before the public warning.'

Nina must decide whether to hold the warning for one more day of sampling, knowing the delay will be scrutinized if contamination spreads, or sign off on the supervisor's draft now. She holds. The next day's sampling returns negative results in the third county, and the four cases are reclassified as a concurrent but independent cluster.
examples.whatToDo: Before updating on a geographic extension in an outbreak investigation, calculate the base rate of false extensions for this pathogen class in comparable outbreak patterns. Apply that base rate as a discount to the new cluster's apparent diagnostic force. The adjusted probability is the update, not the face-value implication of the new cases.
examples.whyItMatters: A single geographic cluster feels like confirmation of broader spread. The base rate of false extensions shows that feeling is often wrong. Moving to 80% on one cluster and then discovering the cluster was independent is the failure mode that explicit update sizing is designed to prevent.

examples.title: Anders strips the dilution effect from a 12-page shipping report and hedges half the position at 73%

planSpec.domain: commodities trader receiving a new shipping disruption report on a grain corridor
planSpec.audience: a grain trader at a commodity desk whose current position is priced around 68% probability of a supply disruption in the next 30 days
planSpec.stakes: a hedging decision worth $500K in premium cost if made now vs. waiting
planSpec.requiredBeat: trader identifies that the 12-page report contains one diagnostic data point amid diluting context; moves from 68% to 73% and hedges half the position

examples.scenario:
You are a grain trader at a commodity desk and the report that just landed in your inbox is twelve pages. The subject line reads 'URGENT: Corridor disruption imminent.' The body opens with satellite imagery, moves to port congestion statistics, names three sources inside the logistics chain, and includes a two-page history of prior disruptions on this corridor.

You have been at 68% probability of supply disruption in the next 30 days. The question is how much this report should move that estimate.

You do what the report does not do for you: you strip the narrative from the diagnostic content.

The satellite imagery shows the same port conditions the last three reports have shown. That is context, not news. The congestion statistics are averages for the past two weeks, which your model already captures. The historical section is background you knew. The three named sources are described but not quoted with new claims.

One sentence in the document contains new diagnostic information: port throughput for the past 48 hours is down 15% from the running average, confirmed by customs clearance data you did not have before.

Port throughput down 15% for 48 hours raises the disruption probability. By how much? Given the volatility of this measure and the base rate of 48-hour throughput dips that do not develop into full disruptions, the move is approximately 5 percentage points. You are now at 73%.

You hedge half the position. Not the full position: the probability is 73%, not 90%. You hedge the half that reflects the elevated probability rather than the emotional weight of a twelve-page URGENT report.
examples.whatToDo: Before sizing any update from a detailed report, identify explicitly which sentences contain new diagnostic information versus which contain background, repetition, or framing. Count the diagnostic sentences. Size the update to what those sentences establish, not to the total weight of the document.
examples.whyItMatters: A twelve-page report with three named sources and satellite imagery feels like comprehensive intelligence. The diagnostic content is often a fraction of the total. Sizing the update to the full document rather than to the diagnostic sentences is the dilution effect in action: more detail, no more predictive weight, but a much larger move than the evidence warrants.

examples.title: Anna earns a 6-point rise in reserve confidence from one high-grade borehole sample and defers the drilling permit

planSpec.domain: geological survey team adding one new borehole sample to a mineral reserve estimate
planSpec.audience: a mining exploration geologist whose current reserve probability sits at 61%
planSpec.stakes: a drilling permit decision that commits $2M in equipment mobilization
planSpec.requiredBeat: one high-grade borehole moves the estimate from 61% to 67% based on spatial correlation logic; permit deferred until two more samples return

examples.scenario:
At six in the morning, the split core is on the sample tray in the field lab, bright with mineral color. The drilling crew has gathered at the trailer door. This is what a high-grade result looks like.

Anna photographs the sample, logs the depth and grade, and sets a timer. She has been at 61% reserve confidence before this result. The question is not whether this sample is good news. It clearly is. The question is how much it should move the estimate.

The sample is one of eight planned for this drill program. The statistical weight of one sample in an eight-sample program is roughly one-eighth of the intended program's total information value, adjusted for spatial correlation. This deposit class shows high spatial correlation at distances below 200 meters, meaning adjacent boreholes tend to return correlated results. The update weight for one sample is higher than one-eighth because of this correlation, but lower than 'everything has changed' because seven samples remain undrilled.

She runs the adjustment. The single high-grade result moves the reserve confidence from 61% to 67%, reflecting meaningful corroboration from one sample while holding space for the seven that have not returned yet. The drilling permit decision, which commits $2M in equipment mobilization, waits.

'Two more samples,' she tells the project manager. 'If the next two results are consistent with this grade, the estimate is where we need it for permit authorization.'
examples.whatToDo: When a single highly positive data point arrives in a sequential sampling process, calculate its update weight based on where it sits in the planned sample sequence and any correlation structure that makes it more or less representative than a single independent observation. Size the update to the calculated weight, not to the emotional salience of the result.
examples.whyItMatters: A high-grade core sample looks like proof. It is one data point in a planned sequence of eight, with known correlation properties that determine how much evidential weight it carries. Moving from 61% to 90% on one sample would mean treating one observation as though it carries the weight of a completed program. The deferred permit is what proportionate updating looks like when the stakes are $2M.

examples.title: Vincent earns 8 percentage points on range expansion from one uncertain sighting and defers the protection recommendation

planSpec.domain: conservation biologist recording a new habitat observation that seems to shift a species range estimate
planSpec.audience: a field biologist tracking a bird species northward range shift whose current estimate is 55% that the range has expanded beyond the historical boundary
planSpec.stakes: whether to recommend emergency habitat protection for a corridor that would cost a development project $8M
planSpec.requiredBeat: one uncertain sighting moves the estimate from 55% to 63% based on misidentification base rate; protection recommendation deferred pending second confirmed sighting with nesting evidence

examples.scenario:
What does a single blurry photograph of a bird 30 kilometers north of its historical range actually tell you about whether that range has permanently expanded?

Vincent is asking that question in the field, camera screen still on, looking at an image that has the right field marks at the right distance but also enough blur at the wingtip to introduce genuine doubt. The field marks are consistent with the target species. The location is 30 kilometers beyond the historical boundary. If confirmed, this sighting would be the strongest evidence yet of the northward range expansion he has been tracking at 55% probability.

But 'if confirmed' is doing a lot of work.

The base rate of misidentification at this range and lighting condition for this species pair runs at roughly 15% to 20%, based on documentation records for comparable photographs. A field photograph with ambiguous wingtip resolution carries a credibility discount that a confirmed, close-range sighting does not.

He calculates: the sighting is real and suggestive. The misidentification discount reduces its diagnostic weight. The absence of breeding evidence at the site reduces it further. The move from 55% is real but limited: the range expansion estimate rises to 63%.

The protection recommendation, which would trigger an $8M development hold, requires two independent confirmed sightings with nesting evidence before it can be defensible. Vincent must decide right now whether to escalate on this single ambiguous photograph and trigger the development hold, or flag the location for a follow-up survey without escalating. He flags the location and does not escalate.
examples.whatToDo: Before updating on a single field observation with ambiguous quality, apply the base rate of misidentification for this species-pair, lighting condition, and observer type as an explicit discount to the apparent diagnostic force of the sighting. The update is from the credibility-adjusted value, not from the face-value implication of the observation.
examples.whyItMatters: A photograph that looks right is not the same as a confirmed sighting. The misidentification base rate exists because photographs that look right are sometimes wrong, and a decision about an $8M development hold cannot rest on the emotional weight of a single ambiguous image. Moving from 55% to 90% on one photograph would mean treating that photograph as though it carries the weight of a confirmed, independently verified observation.

examples.title: Catarina finds one diagnostic sentence in 47 pages and moves the revenue guidance estimate 4 points downward

planSpec.domain: portfolio manager reviewing a company's earnings call transcript looking for changes to forward guidance
planSpec.audience: a fund manager whose position is sized around a 59% probability of the company meeting annual revenue guidance
planSpec.stakes: whether to increase or reduce a $12M position before the next trading session
planSpec.requiredBeat: 47-page transcript yields one diagnostic sentence; move is from 59% to 55%; position is modestly reduced rather than exited

examples.scenario:
It is two in the morning. Catarina, a portfolio manager at a mid-size fund, has just finished reading the evening's earnings call transcript in her home office, with the market opening in six hours. She had been careful not to trust how she felt after reading it.

Forty-seven pages. The CEO's opening remarks: four pages of backward-looking operational summary, two paragraphs of market context, a page on strategic priorities she had heard on three previous calls. The CFO's section: twelve pages of geographic breakdown, fourteen pages of product line review, eight pages of year-over-year comparisons that matched her model within rounding.

One sentence in the CFO's section had been new. A revision to the geographic revenue guidance for one of three regions, from 'strong growth' to 'growth in line with prior year.' One sentence. Buried in page thirty-one of a forty-seven-page document.

If she had sized the update to the experience of reading 47 dense pages from a company whose prior calls had been uniformly confident, the estimate would have moved more than it should. The experience was heavy. The diagnostic content was light.

She moved from 59% to 55%. One geographic segment had been quietly downgraded by four words. The rest of the call had confirmed what she already knew. The four-point move reflected the weight of those four words, not the weight of the document that carried them.

She must decide before the market opens: exit the position entirely, reduce it modestly, or hold. The question is whether the one-sentence revision warrants a full exit or a proportionate trim. She reduces from $12M to $10M. A full exit would have reflected the emotional weight of 47 pages. The trim reflects the actual diagnostic content of one sentence.
examples.whatToDo: After reading a long document, write down which specific sentences changed your estimate and which confirmed what you already knew. Size the update to the sentences that changed things. Verify that the size of your position change matches the diagnostic weight of those sentences, not the volume or vividness of the surrounding document.
examples.whyItMatters: A 47-page earnings transcript read late at night feels like a comprehensive intelligence update. The diagnostic content was one sentence. The position change that matched the one sentence was 4 percentage points and a $2M reduction. A position change that matched the document's overall volume would have been much larger and would not have been calibrated to what the evidence actually said.

questions.prompt: Ryan, a defense attorney, receives a six-page witness statement that strongly supports her client's case. Her first instinct is to move her acquittal estimate from 45% to 70%. After checking the witness's history and finding a prior impeachment on a related matter, she moves to 51% instead. What approach does Ryan's process illustrate, and why does it matter?
choices: Sizing each update to match the actual diagnostic weight of the new evidence rather than its emotional salience, volume, or the strength of the narrative it is embedded in.
Making consistently equal-sized updates in response to each new piece of incoming information as the best available method for avoiding anchoring bias.
Updating beliefs more frequently and aggressively in fast-moving situations in order to avoid the problem of holding stale, outdated positions.
questions.explanation: Proportionate revision requires distinguishing how strongly you feel about new information from how much diagnostic weight that information actually carries. A vivid, confident witness statement may feel like it demands a 25-point move when the evidence, adjusted for credibility concerns, warrants a 6-point move. A 12-page report may feel comprehensive when it contains one diagnostic sentence. The skill is in extracting the actual evidentiary weight and moving by exactly that amount.

questions.prompt: A defense attorney receives a witness statement that strongly supports the defense narrative but comes from a witness who was impeached on a prior inconsistency in a different case. Her current acquittal estimate is 45%. She calculates that the statement, from a clean witness, would be worth roughly a 20-point move. Which update is most calibrated to the available evidence?
choices: Moving to 70% because the statement directly and strongly supports the defense narrative and should be taken at its full face value.
Staying at 45% because any witness statement from a previously impeachable source must be entirely discounted and cannot move the estimate at all.
Moving to approximately 51% after applying a credibility discount that reflects the impeachment risk reducing the statement's evidential weight by roughly half.
questions.explanation: The statement has real evidential value, but a witness who can be impeached on a prior inconsistency has reduced credibility weight. Discounting the full 20-point value by roughly half produces the 51% estimate. Moving to 70% would treat the statement as fully credible. Staying at 45% would treat it as worthless. Neither is calibrated to the actual evidence: a real statement with a real credibility limitation.

questions.prompt: An epidemiologist tracking a foodborne illness cluster discovers a new geographically distinct cluster of four cases in a third county. The base rate of false geographic extensions for this pathogen class is 25% to 30%. Her current estimate of broader regional contamination is 35%. She is being pressed for an immediate public warning. Which update best reflects the evidence?
choices: Moving immediately to 90% probability of broader contamination and issuing the warning, because four confirmed cases in a new county are strong evidence of regional spread.
Staying at 35% because the base rate of false extensions means the new cluster is more likely to be independent than connected.
Moving to approximately 42% and recommending one more day of sampling before issuing the warning, because the cluster raises the probability meaningfully but does not reach the warning threshold.
questions.explanation: The 25-30% base rate of false geographic extensions means a single new cluster is not conclusive evidence of broader spread. The probability should rise, reflecting that one real cluster is more consistent with regional contamination than zero clusters. Moving to 90% would treat four cases in one county as equivalent to definitive evidence of regional spread. The 42% estimate reflects the update the evidence warrants while keeping the warning threshold appropriately higher.

questions.prompt: Bill Flack moved his estimate on the Arafat polonium story by 5 percentage points rather than 30 or more. What does this specific update size demonstrate about the relationship between signal strength and update size?
choices: That the update was calibrated to what the evidence had actually established: a meaningful but not conclusive finding that warranted a proportionate move rather than a dramatic revision.
That Flack was being excessively cautious and should have moved his estimate far more aggressively given the seriousness and credibility of the new signal.
That small updates are inherently better than large ones in all forecasting contexts, regardless of how strong or decisive the supporting evidence actually is.
questions.explanation: The polonium finding was suggestive, not conclusive. The investigation had not returned a final determination, and the possibility of incidental rather than administered exposure was real. Moving 5 points acknowledged that a real investigation had found a real result while recognizing that the result did not establish the conclusion the headline implied. A 30-point move would have implied far greater certainty than the evidence warranted. Five points was what the evidence had earned.

questions.prompt: A trader receives a 12-page report marked URGENT that includes satellite imagery, port congestion data, named sources, and historical context. After stripping the narrative from the diagnostic content, she finds one new data point: port throughput down 15% for 48 hours. She moves from 68% to 73% rather than to 90%. What does this pattern illustrate?
choices: That satellite imagery and named sources are inherently unreliable in commodity forecasting contexts and should never factor into probability estimates.
That the trader is systematically underreacting to genuinely strong evidence because she has not learned to appropriately trust comprehensive, well-sourced reports.

That the dilution effect can be neutralized by explicitly separating diagnostic content from contextual background before sizing the update, producing a move that matches the evidence rather than the document's volume.
questions.explanation: The dilution effect occurs when a detailed, narrative-rich document inflates the perceived strength of the evidence it contains. The satellite imagery, named sources, and historical context add volume and vividness without adding diagnostic force beyond the one new data point. Stripping the narrative before sizing the update allows the trader to move by exactly what the one new data point warrants: approximately 5 percentage points. Moving to 90% would have matched the document's emotional weight rather than its diagnostic content.

questions.prompt: A geologist has planned an eight-borehole drill program to reach 80% reserve confidence. The first borehole returns a high-grade result. Given high spatial correlation in this deposit class, the first result carries more weight than one-eighth of the planned program but less than the full program's total information value. The current estimate is 61%. Which update is most calibrated to the evidence?
choices: Moving immediately to 90% because a single high-grade first borehole result represents the strongest possible early positive signal in this context.
Moving from 61% to 67%, reflecting that one spatially correlated result warrants a meaningful but bounded update given that seven samples remain undrilled.
Staying at 61% because no probability update is appropriate or defensible until the full eight-sample drilling program is entirely complete.
questions.explanation: One high-grade result in a spatially correlated deposit carries more evidential weight than one-eighth of the planned program but cannot substitute for the remaining seven samples. Moving to 90% would treat one result as though it carries the weight of a completed program. Staying at 61% would ignore genuine positive evidence. Moving to 67% reflects the calibrated update: meaningful corroboration from one result that warrants a bounded move while preserving seven opportunities to update further.

questions.prompt: Tim Minto's forecasting log shows a gentle staircase of small, proportionate updates over months, while a colleague's log shows long flat stretches followed by sharp jumps whenever a major headline arrives. Both forecasters reach similar final estimates on many questions. Which pattern produces better calibration across the full life of a question, and why?
choices: Because frequent small updates visibly demonstrate intellectual engagement with the forecasting question and signal professional credibility and diligence to other forecasters.
Because small, incremental updates are less likely to draw critical attention from supervisors who might otherwise question the analyst's conviction or analytical consistency.
Because small proportionate updates keep the estimate calibrated throughout the question's life rather than leaving it systematically wrong during the long periods between major signals.
questions.explanation: A forecaster who holds an estimate steady through accumulating evidence and then corrects sharply when overwhelmed produces two calibration errors in sequence: anchoring during the holding period and overcorrection at the point of revision. If a question is live for 90 days and the estimate is wrong for 60 of them before a dramatic correction, the track record across the full period is poor regardless of the final accuracy. Minto's small proportionate updates kept the estimate close to the true probability at each step.

questions.prompt: A fund manager reads a 47-page earnings transcript and finds one sentence of genuinely revised guidance buried on page 31. She moves from 59% to 55% probability of meeting annual revenue targets. What is the correct way to verify that this update was proportionate?
choices: Count the total pages read and size the position change proportionate to document length relative to the average earnings call.
Check that the size of the estimate change and the position change both correspond to the diagnostic weight of the one revised sentence rather than to the total volume of the document.
Move to 30% probability because a management team that buries a guidance revision on page 31 of a 47-page document has shown poor disclosure behavior.
questions.explanation: Proportionality requires that the update reflect what the evidence established: one geographic segment had been quietly downgraded in its growth outlook. That is worth a moderate downward revision to the revenue guidance probability, not a dramatic one. Checking that the estimate move (4 points) and position change ($2M from $12M) match the diagnostic weight of one sentence is the calibration check. Sizing either to the total document length or to interpretations of management behavior substitutes emotional reaction for evidential reasoning.

questions.prompt: An organization's forecasting culture consistently rewards analysts who make large, confident revisions in response to major news events and treats small proportionate updates as timid. Over time, what effect does this culture have on forecast quality?
choices: It systematically degrades calibration by training analysts to size updates to emotional salience rather than diagnostic weight, producing estimates that move too far on vivid signals and not enough on quiet ones.
It improves forecast quality over time by ensuring that analysts do not anchor too rigidly to prior estimates and remain willing to make bold, decisive revisions when major events warrant them.
It has no meaningful systematic effect because individual analyst skill and professional judgment reliably compensate for whatever reward structures the organization puts in place.
questions.explanation: When bold revisions are rewarded regardless of whether they were warranted by the evidence, analysts learn to perform conviction rather than to calibrate. They move large on vivid, emotionally resonant signals because that is what gets acknowledged, and small on quiet signals that actually carry more diagnostic weight. Over time, the estimates from such a culture systematically overreact to dramatic news and underreact to incremental evidence, which is the opposite of what calibrated updating requires.

reviewCards.front: What is proportionate revision and why does update size matter as much as update frequency?
reviewCards.back: Proportionate revision means moving an estimate by the amount the new evidence has actually earned, not by its emotional salience or the volume of detail it arrives with. Update frequency matters less than update sizing: a forecaster who updates frequently with poorly sized moves is not more accurate than one who updates less often with precisely calibrated ones.

reviewCards.front: What is the dilution effect, and how does it distort update sizing?
reviewCards.back: The dilution effect occurs when a detail-rich document makes an estimate feel like it has received more diagnostic information than it actually has. The mind cannot easily separate 'this contains a lot of information' from 'this contains a lot of information that actually changes the estimate.' The result is updates sized to the volume and vividness of the document rather than to the specific sentences that contain new diagnostic content.

reviewCards.front: What did Bill Flack's 5-percentage-point revision on the Arafat polonium story demonstrate?
reviewCards.back: That proportionate revision is not timidity. The polonium finding was meaningful but not conclusive, and a 5-point move reflected what the evidence had established rather than what the headline implied. Moving dramatically would have granted the story more evidentiary force than it had. Moving not at all would have ignored genuine evidence. Five points was accurate.

reviewCards.front: What distinguished Tim Minto's forecasting pattern from hold-and-revise forecasters?
reviewCards.back: Minto made many small proportionate updates rather than holding estimates stable and then correcting sharply. His estimates remained calibrated throughout the full life of a question rather than only at the moment of resolution. Hold-and-revise forecasters produce two calibration errors in sequence: anchoring during the holding period, then overcorrection at the point of forced revision.

reviewCards.front: What is the correct sequence for sizing an update from a detailed document?
reviewCards.back: Identify the diagnostic sentences before reading the full document. After reading, verify that the update is sized to those sentences rather than to the total volume, vividness, or emotional weight of the surrounding document. The check is: does the estimate move match what the diagnostic sentences established?

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Before sizing any update, identify the specific evidence that warrants the move and calculate how much that evidence, adjusted for its credibility and base rates, actually changes the estimate. Move by that amount rather than by the emotional salience of how the information arrived.

ifThenPlans.context: When new information arrives that feels like it demands a large update
ifThenPlans.plan: If the new information is vivid, confident, or comes with many supporting details, then strip the narrative from the diagnostic content before sizing the move. Ask: what is the single new fact this information establishes, and how much does that fact alone change the probability?

ifThenPlans.context: When reviewing a long report, transcript, or document that contains an update
ifThenPlans.plan: If the document is longer than a few pages, then identify the specific sentences that contain new diagnostic information. After reading, verify that the update is sized to those sentences, not to the total length or vividness of the document.

ifThenPlans.context: When a credibility concern limits the evidential weight of new information
ifThenPlans.plan: If the source has known reliability limitations or prior impeachment, then apply the credibility discount explicitly before the update rather than letting it get overlooked when the information feels strong.

ifThenPlans.context: When updating regularly on a question over many days or weeks
ifThenPlans.plan: If a new signal arrives, then move by the amount the signal warrants rather than waiting for certainty before revising. Small proportionate updates are more accurate over the full life of a question than long stable periods followed by large corrections.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: The next time you receive a detailed report or message, count the sentences that contain genuinely new diagnostic information versus the sentences that provide context, repetition, or framing. Write both counts. Then ask: if you had received only the diagnostic sentences, what would your update have been? Compare that to what you actually felt after reading the full document.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, when you update an estimate or belief, write down the specific evidence that triggered the move and calculate whether the size of the move matches the credibility-adjusted weight of that evidence. Over time, compare your actual update sizes to what you later calculate they should have been. The pattern of over- or under-updating is the thing to correct.

memorableLines.text: The new evidence did not change the story. It added one small piece to it. The estimate moved by exactly as much as that piece earned.
memorableLines.why: It names the proportionate revision principle in three consecutive sentences that each carry a distinct step: the evidence was real, it was bounded, and the move matched the bound.

memorableLines.text: Flack's 5-percentage-point revision was not timid. It was accurate. The polonium story was suggestive, not conclusive, and a 5-point move was what the evidence had earned.
memorableLines.why: It reframes proportionate revision as accuracy rather than timidity, and names the specific move (5 points) alongside the specific reason (suggestive but not conclusive) to make the principle concrete.

memorableLines.text: Tim Minto's forecasting log looked like a gentle staircase: many small steps rather than the cliffs and plateaus that mark a forecaster who holds and then panics.
memorableLines.why: The staircase image makes the pattern visible and distinguishes it from its failure mode in a single sentence.
